title: Indian H-1B Buyers Made North Texas the Hottest Housing Market in America. Now They're Gone.
excerpt: Home prices in Dallas's Collin County have fallen 9% as Trump's visa crackdown, a $100,000 H-1B fee, and mass tech layoffs drive Indian buyers out of the market
body:
For years, the suburbs north of Dallas were ground zero for one of America's most extraordinary housing booms. Subdivisions multiplied. Prices soared. Builders could not put up homes fast enough. The engine behind it all: a wave of Indian-born H-1B visa workers flooding into high-paying tech jobs along the corporate corridor that attracted more company headquarters than anywhere else in the country.

Now that engine has stalled — and the effects are rippling out in ways that matter far beyond Texas.

Home prices in Collin County, the suburban epicentre of the boom, fell nearly 9% year-over-year as of February, more than double the 4% drop across the broader Dallas-Fort Worth metro, according to Redfin data. The retreat of Indian buyers from the market is functioning like a release valve on one of the most overheated regional housing markets in the country.

## How Indian Buyers Built North Texas

The federal government granted nearly 32,000 new H-1B approvals in the Dallas area alone during the Biden administration — topping Silicon Valley, Seattle, San Francisco, and Washington, D.C. Only New York ranked higher, according to a Bloomberg investigation citing USCIS data.

The workers who arrived on those visas poured into new subdivisions in Prosper, Frisco, and Celina. Collin County's Indian-born population surged from an average of 70,000 annually to over 116,000 in the five years through 2024. In Frisco alone — a city of 235,000 — the share of Indian residents jumped from 6% to nearly 20%.

Builders tailored homes to this clientele. Zach Schneider of Tradition Homes designed model homes with north-facing "puja" rooms for Hindu prayer and optional "spice kitchens" for buyers from India. At peak demand, South Asian buyers represented 70% of his company's sales. That figure has now fallen below 30%, even as he sits on a backlog of 125 luxury homes under construction.

## The Policy Crackdown

Trump's escalating restrictions on the H-1B programme have systematically dismantled the conditions that made North Texas a magnet for Indian tech talent.

In September 2025, Trump signed a proclamation imposing a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions — a measure that effectively priced out the staffing firms and mid-tier tech contractors that had been the biggest sponsors of Indian workers in Dallas. The Labour Department launched "Project Firewall," an enforcement initiative targeting employer abuse.

The administration also barred non-permanent residents, including H-1B holders, from FHA-insured mortgages. The share of FHA loan volume going to non-permanent residents dropped from 6% to virtually zero within months.

At the state level, Governor Greg Abbott froze new H-1B petitions by state agencies and public universities. Attorney General Ken Paxton launched investigations into nearly 30 North Texas businesses suspected of visa fraud.

## The Human Cost

In the Mustang Lakes subdivision in Celina, Ravi Vavilala — an Indian-born naturalized citizen — bought a five-bedroom home for $895,000 in late 2023. He was laid off from his IT job in March. The house is now listed at $873,000, below what he paid, and he is struggling to compete against builder incentives down the street.

Before his next showing, Vavilala moved his religious items out of sight. "Because the market is very slow, I want to attract all types of buyers," he told Bloomberg.

Real estate agent Neeraj Gupta, who arrived in Dallas on an H-1B visa in 2000, says his phone — once ringing constantly with buyers — now rings with sellers looking to cut losses. Some clients are absorbing monthly rental losses of $300 to $1,500. One senior IT director holding two Frisco homes worth over $1 million each is weighing a move back to India.

Another financed an $800,000 home almost entirely with debt; the property is now worth less than the loan balance. "He will not lose anything," Gupta said. "The banks will lose."

## What Comes Next

Immigration attorney Sharadha Kodem, based in Frisco, says the anxiety among her clients is unlike anything in her career. H-1B holders who bought homes in remote suburbs while working remotely are now being called back to offices in Dallas — or told to relocate to Seattle or San Francisco. Those who are laid off have just 60 days to find a new sponsor before their visa status lapses.

Housing analyst Alex Barron warned that the exit of South Asian buyers leaves a gap with no obvious replacement. "These H-1B visas are the number one converters of potential homebuyers to actual homebuyers," he said. "But when you get fewer people receiving H-1B visas, you get an immediate negative surprise because you have housing that has already been built for those people sitting on the market."

With over 123,000 tech jobs cut in the first half of 2026 and AI cited as the primary driver, the pressure on Indian workers in America is coming from multiple directions at once.

The pattern is not unique to the United States. Canada capped international students in 2024 to ease housing pressure. Spain halted its golden visa programme for property buyers. Switzerland will hold a referendum on a population cap this summer.

But the scale of what happened in North Texas — and the speed of the reversal — is a warning sign for every American metro where skilled immigrants have been quietly propping up the housing market.

*Sources: New York Post, Bloomberg, Redfin, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Pew Research Center*
